periods.activity_title: From Winning Obsession to Joyful Play: First Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read — pre-reading activity (p.103): paired talk on games played for fun versus competition.
Let us discuss — Part I (p.105): True/False and short-answer questions on Prabhat's character.

time_bands.activity: Open with the pre-reading warm-up from “Let us read” (p.103): ask students which games they play for fun and which for competition, then take a quick class poll. Briefly clarify the vocabulary — friendly matches, opponent, sporting spirit — using students' own suggestions before confirming the textbook meanings.

Read the story aloud together — teacher reads with expression while students follow in their books (p.103–105, Part I). Pause at key moments: when Prabhat decides to alter the scoreboard and when Surya reacts to losing without distress.

Work through “Let us discuss” Part I (p.105) as a whole-class discussion: the True/False statement about Prabhat accepting defeat, the special significance of the last Friday of each month, and who kept the score. Invite two or three students to share their view on whether Prabhat would want a rematch.

periods.teacher_notes: Prabhat's compulsive need to win — choosing only games he knows he will win — is the moral engine of the whole story; draw this out during the True/False discussion so students feel the tension before the cheating episode. A common pitfall here is treating the pre-reading vocabulary items as a separate writing exercise; keep them oral and brisk so the bulk of time goes to reading the story aloud.

periods.activity_title: Surya's Joy, Prabhat's Guilt: Close Reading and Reflection

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss — Part II (p.107): short-answer questions on Surya's attitude and what Prabhat observes.
Let us think and reflect — I (p.108): extract analysis on Prabhat's selective participation and his sleepless night.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect — II (p.108): choose any two extended-response questions on sporting spirit and the title's meaning.

time_bands.activity: Continue reading the story aloud (p.105–107, Part II) with students following, pausing at the moment Prabhat secretly changes the scoreboard and at Surya's cheerful concession of defeat.

Discuss the two “Let us discuss” Part II questions (p.107) in pairs, then share with the class: how Surya felt about playing, and what specific quality of Surya's Prabhat found himself observing day after day.

Work through the extract from “Let us think and reflect” I (p.108): students complete the sentence about when Prabhat plays, identify the game he excels at, and choose the option that best describes his behaviour. Then tackle the second extract — selecting the word for how Prabhat felt that night and explaining why Surya's reaction surprised him — as a short written response before a brief whole-class share-out.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read of Surya's delight in basketball despite playing poorly, students are now positioned to feel the contrast with Prabhat's guilt-ridden ‘victory’; keep the discussion anchored in those two contrasting reactions rather than moving to abstract moralising. The extract analysis in “Let us think and reflect” I requires careful reading of the specific passage, so allow an unhurried reading aloud of each extract before students attempt the sub-questions. The extended-response questions in “Let us think and reflect” II are rich but time-consuming; they are set as self-study so students can think carefully in writing.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — first listen (p.110): circle the chess pair from three options after hearing the announcement.
Let us listen — second listen (p.110): fill notes on match count, notice board content, sponsor, scorekeeper, referee, and kho-kho periods.
Let us speak (p.111): paired role-plays using please, thank you, and sorry across two or three assigned situations.

time_bands.activity: Set the context: tell students they will hear a school sports announcement. Read the transcript (p.128) aloud clearly and at a natural pace while students listen and circle the chess pair from the three options given (p.110).

Read the announcement a second time at the same pace. Students fill in their notes on the six details: number of Friday matches, what is on the notice board, the kho-kho sponsor, the chess scorekeeper, the kho-kho referee, and the periods set aside for kho-kho (p.110). Check answers as a class immediately after.

Introduce the “Let us speak” task (p.111): briefly model one situation using the prompt table, showing how to frame a request with ‘please’ and a sincere apology with ‘sorry’. Pairs choose two or three situations from the list, rehearse briefly, then two or three pairs perform their exchanges for the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The announcement mentions kho-kho, chess, and badminton — the same sports students encountered in the story — so a quick connection to Prabhat's badminton match helps students engage with the listening context. Watch for students who fill in answers from memory rather than from listening; encourage them to keep pencils down until the second reading begins. In the speaking activity, students sometimes confuse a polite request with a command; the prompt table on p.111 gives the scaffold, so direct hesitant students to it rather than letting them go silent.

periods.activity_title: Prabhat's Diary and the Language of Actions Past

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.112): complete Prabhat's diary entry by placing eight given phrases in the correct blanks.
Let us learn — circle the verbs (p.109): identify verbs in three sentences from the story.
Let us learn — arrange verbs into Column A and B (p.109): sort circled verbs into first action (past perfect) and second action (simple past).
Let us learn — fill blanks with past perfect (p.109): complete five sentences using the past perfect form of bracketed verbs.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the diary entry task (p.112): read Prabhat's incomplete diary aloud with the class, then ask students what emotion is missing from each blank before they write. Students complete the diary individually using the eight phrases in the box, then a volunteer reads the finished entry aloud for class verification.

Transition to “Let us learn” (p.109): read the three story sentences on the board together and ask students to circle the verbs, identifying both the ‘had + past participle’ forms and the simple past forms. Introduce the term ‘past perfect’ by asking which action happened first in each sentence.

Students complete the Column A / Column B sorting table (p.109), placing each circled verb under ‘first action’ or ‘second action’. Then they fill in the five past-perfect sentences (p.109) independently, using the bracketed verbs as a guide. The last two minutes are a quick class check of answers.

periods.teacher_notes: The diary entry connects directly to the moral moment of the story — Prabhat's guilt after cheating — so students should have a clear emotional anchor before filling in the blanks. The most common error in the past-perfect task is using simple past where past perfect is needed; drawing a brief timeline on the board (action 1 → action 2) for sentence 1 before students attempt the rest prevents this confusion. The word-building puzzle task in “Let us learn” is left as a self-study activity for students who enjoy wordplay.
materials: Textbook, p.109 and p.112; board or chart for verb timeline

periods.activity_title: Sporting Heroes: Reading Bio-Sketches and Exploring Arjuna Awardees

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.113–114): read Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra bio-sketches; discuss qualities that drove their success.

time_bands.activity: Students read the bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra (p.113–114) silently, then one student reads each sketch aloud. Ask the class to underline any phrases that describe qualities of character or attitude as they listen.

Small-group discussion (three or four students per group): what personal qualities — beyond talent — helped each sportsperson succeed despite humble or difficult beginnings? Groups identify at least two qualities per person and connect them to the idea of sporting spirit explored in Prabhat and Surya's story.

Each group shares one quality they found most striking; the teacher records these on the board in two columns (Deepika / Neeraj). Close by asking students to name one quality from the board that they saw in Surya — connecting the real-world athletes to the story's theme of joyful, honest participation.

periods.teacher_notes: The bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra are designed to extend the story's theme of sporting spirit into real-world achievement, so keep the discussion anchored in character and attitude rather than drifting into factual recall of medals and dates. A rich extension — researching further Arjuna Awardees from the link on p.114 — is noted here as a self-study pointer for students who wish to explore independently outside class.

items.source_lo: Student reads a narrative prose text closely, identifying character motivation, inference, and thematic significance using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Prabhat's compulsive winning, Surya's joyful play, cheating, guilt, sporting spirit transformation.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about Prabhat at the beginning of the story. Mark each statement True or False.
1. Prabhat would refuse to play a game if he felt he might lose.
2. Prabhat chose games based on whether he was certain to win them.
3. Prabhat played every game with a relaxed and carefree attitude.
4. Prabhat altered the scoreboard because he genuinely believed he was winning.

options.text: Prabhat would refuse to play a game if he felt he might lose.
Prabhat chose games based on whether he was certain to win them.
Prabhat played every game with a relaxed and carefree attitude.
Prabhat altered the scoreboard because he genuinely believed he was winning.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — Prabhat participated only when he was sure of winning.
2. True — He avoided games where there was a risk of losing.
3. False — Prabhat played with fierce seriousness, never relaxed.
4. False — He changed the scoreboard because he realised he was about to lose, not because he believed he was winning.

items.source_lo: Student reads a narrative prose text closely, identifying character motivation, inference, and thematic significance using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Prabhat's compulsive winning, Surya's joyful play, cheating, guilt, sporting spirit transformation.
items.item_stem: In the story, Prabhat wins the badminton match against Surya but cannot sleep that night, and in the days that follow he quietly watches Surya play basketball — a game Surya is poor at — yet Surya's enjoyment never fades. What does this contrast reveal about the difference between Prabhat's idea of sport and Surya's? What does Prabhat's sleeplessness suggest about the insight he is beginning to reach?

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Prabhat measures sport by its outcome — winning — while Surya finds value in the act of playing itself, regardless of the score. Prabhat's sleeplessness reveals that he is starting to sense, however uneasily, that the guilt of cheating and the sight of Surya's contentment point to something he has been missing: the pleasure of honest, wholehearted participation.

items.item_stem:
Your teacher will read the school sports announcement aloud. Listen carefully and choose the correct answer for each question.

1. How many matches will be played this Friday?
A. Two
B. Three
C. Four
D. Five

2. Which club is sponsoring the refreshments for the kho-kho team?
A. Sunrise Sports Club
B. Xydium Sports Club
C. Eagle Sports Club
D. Victory Sports Club

3. Who will serve as the referee for the kho-kho match?
A. Vani
B. Sarita
C. The sports teacher
D. Nupur

what_each_option_reveals.A: Students who choose this may have heard only the matches described in detail and missed the opening count.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Suggests the student confused the number of periods mentioned (2nd and 3rd) with match count.
what_each_option_reveals.D: No basis in the announcement; likely a random guess.

teacher_guide.note: This item covers question 1 only. Questions 2 and 3 from the stem are SCR in intent; for the MCQ format above, only question 1 is classified MCQ. See Q-LIS-A-2 for the fill-in component covering details 2 and 3.

Detail | Answer

Who is the scorekeeper for chess? | _______________
Where will the badminton match be held? | _______________
During which periods will kho-kho be played? | _______________

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. The chess match will be held in the 1st floor activity room.

4. Kho-kho will be played during the 2nd and 3rd periods.

items.item_stem: You are a student in the school from the story. A classmate has been practising with you every day to help you prepare for the Inter-House badminton match. Speak to your classmate: thank them sincerely for their help and explain one way their support made a difference to your game. Use the word 'thank you' appropriately in your response.

expected_elements: Uses 'thank you' or 'I am grateful' clearly and sincerely.
Names one specific way the classmate's help improved their game.
Speaks in complete sentences with natural fluency.
Maintains a warm, polite tone throughout.

items.source_lo: Student uses courteous language — request, apology, gratitude — appropriately in paired spoken exchanges using guided conversation as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Role-play situations using please, thank you, and sorry; classroom and school social contexts.
items.item_stem: Imagine you are Prabhat, the day after the badminton match. You realise you acted unfairly by secretly changing the scoreboard. Approach Surya and apologise to him in your own words. In your apology, admit what you did wrong, explain why it was unfair to Surya, and tell him what you will do differently next time. Use 'sorry' appropriately and give a reason for your action.

expected_elements: Uses 'sorry' clearly with a genuine, not casual, tone.
Admits the specific wrong — changing the scoreboard secretly.
Explains why the action was unfair to Surya as an opponent.
States a commitment to honest play in future matches.

items.source_lo: Student completes a guided functional writing task — a personal diary entry — organising given phrases coherently to express a character's emotional experience using prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Prabhat's diary entry the night after cheating: guilt, surprise at Surya's contentment, emotional conflict.
items.item_stem:
Prabhat's diary entry from the night after the badminton match captures his guilt and confusion. Below is a short diary entry written by Surya on the same evening. Some phrases from the box are missing. Choose the correct phrase from the box to complete each blank so that Surya's entry reads clearly and naturally.

Phrases: [I had a wonderful time / I cannot understand why he seemed so upset / I hope we can play again / winning was not the most important thing / I tried my best throughout the match]

Dear Diary,
Today I played badminton against Prabhat. 1. _______________ and played with all my energy. Even though the final score did not go my way, 2. _______________. For me, 3. _______________ — enjoying the game is what matters. What puzzled me was that Prabhat looked troubled after the match. 4. _______________. 5. _______________ soon — it was really fun!

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. I tried my best throughout the match
2. I had a wonderful time
3. winning was not the most important thing
4. I cannot understand why he seemed so upset
5. I hope we can play again

items.source_context: Prabhat's diary entry the night after cheating: guilt, surprise at Surya's contentment, emotional conflict.
items.item_stem: By the end of the story, Prabhat has changed. He joins games like hide-and-seek with genuine enthusiasm, cracks jokes during badminton, and earns the compliment of great sporting spirit from his classmates. Write a diary entry of about 80–100 words from Prabhat's point of view, describing how he now feels about playing games and what changed his thinking. Use the first person ('I') and write as Prabhat.

expected_elements: Written in first person as Prabhat, diary format.
Mentions a specific change — joining games he would have avoided.
Connects Surya's joyful attitude as the turning point.
Expresses how enjoying the game now matters more than winning.

items.item_stem: Match each sentence from the story of Prabhat and Surya in Column A with the correct description of the underlined verb in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A — Sentence | Column B — Description of the underlined verb

The class was discussing how Prabhat had played so well. | Past perfect — an action completed before another past action

items.source_context: Past perfect tense: identifying verbs in story sentences, sorting first/second actions, forming had + past participle.
items.item_stem:
The sentences below describe events from the story of Prabhat and Surya. Each sentence has two events. Rewrite the sentence by joining the two events with 'before' or 'by the time', using the past perfect tense for the earlier event. The first one is done as an example.

Example: Prabhat changed the scoreboard. Then Surya noticed.
→ Prabhat had already changed the scoreboard before Surya noticed.

1. Surya joined the school. He did not know Prabhat.
2. Prabhat observed Surya playing basketball for many days. Then he understood Surya's attitude.
3. Surya played several games. He remained cheerful throughout.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. Before Surya joined the school, he had never met Prabhat. (or: Surya had not known Prabhat before he joined the school.) 2. By the time Prabhat understood Surya's attitude, he had observed him playing basketball for many days. 3. By the time Surya finished playing several games, he had remained cheerful throughout. (Accept reasonable variations that correctly use past perfect for the earlier action.)

items.item_stem: The bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra in the textbook (p.113–114) describe two athletes who rose to international success despite difficult early circumstances. From the two bio-sketches, identify one quality that both athletes share and explain, with evidence from the sketches, how that quality helped each of them succeed. Write your response in about 60–80 words.

expected_elements: Names one quality shared by both athletes (e.g., determination, perseverance).
Provides evidence from Deepika Kumari's bio-sketch to support the quality.
Provides evidence from Neeraj Chopra's bio-sketch to support the quality.
Links the shared quality to success despite humble or difficult beginnings.

items.source_context: Bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra; Arjuna Awardees; qualities enabling success despite humble beginnings.
items.item_stem: Using the bio-sketches of Deepika Kumari and Neeraj Chopra (p.113–114) as your starting point, choose ONE Arjuna Awardee from India who plays a sport different from archery or javelin throw. Research their sporting journey and prepare a short bio-sketch of about 100 words. Your sketch should include: the sport they play, one challenge they overcame, one achievement they are known for, and one quality of character or sporting spirit you most admire in them.

expected_elements: Names a specific Arjuna Awardee and their sport clearly.
Describes one genuine challenge or humble beginning they faced.
States one specific, well-known achievement.
Identifies a quality of character or sporting spirit with a brief justification.
